entry.title: OFAC adds Monero (XMR) and 100+ TRON addresses to ISIS-K SDN entry; designates Brazilian payments company Pixwave under SDGT and narco-trafficking EO

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)

entry.content:
On July 1, 2026, OFAC published two actions on its recent-actions page. First, OFAC updated the existing Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) entry for ISIS-K (Islamic State Khorasan Province / ISIL Khorasan) to add three Monero (XMR) cryptocurrency wallet addresses and more than 100 TRON (TRC-20) blockchain addresses — including USDT-TRC20 stablecoin addresses — to the SDN List. US persons and virtual asset service providers are prohibited from transacting with SDN-listed addresses; crypto exchanges with XMR or TRX-chain exposure (including USDT-TRC20) must immediately screen and block these addresses under 31 C.F.R. Part 594 and E.O. 13224. Second, OFAC designated Pixwave Soluções de Pagamentos Ltda, a Brazilian payment-technology company, under the SDGT authority (E.O. 13224) and Executive Order 14059 (ILLICIT-DRUGS-EO14059), alleging Pixwave provided payment-processing services to the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), a Brazilian narco-trafficking organization. Both designations are effective July 1, 2026.
Primary source: OFAC Recent Actions — July 1, 2026 (primary source; retrieved) — https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20260701
Relevant to: crypto exchanges, virtual asset service providers (VASPs), payment processors, money transmitters, and any US person transacting in Monero or TRON-chain assets (including USDT-TRC20)

entry.title: SEC seeks public comment on registration and disclosure rules for novel exchange-traded funds (Release 33-11426) — crypto-asset and event-contract ETFs expressly in scope

category.term: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

entry.content:
On June 30, 2026, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission released Release 33-11426, a request for public comment on potential amendments to its registration and disclosure rules for novel types of exchange-traded funds, including crypto-asset ETFs and ETFs holding event-contract or prediction-market exposures. The release asks whether current disclosure frameworks adequately address risks specific to non-standard ETF product types and whether the Commission should take additional steps, including potential Commission-initiated delay of automatic effectiveness of registration statements under Rule 485. Comments are due 60 days after Federal Register publication.

entry.title: SCOTUS rules 6-3 that for-cause removal protections for SEC and CFTC commissioners are unconstitutional — Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332)

category.term: U.S. Supreme Court

entry.content:
On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332), holding 6-3 that the Federal Trade Commission's for-cause removal provision (15 U.S.C. §41) is 'contrary to the separation of powers enshrined in the Constitution.' Authored by Chief Justice Roberts, the ruling overturns Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935), a 91-year precedent that had permitted Congress to insulate independent agency commissioners from at-will presidential removal. Because the SEC and CFTC operate under structurally identical removal protections, the holding applies to them as well — meaning the President may now remove SEC and CFTC commissioners without cause, effective immediately. In a companion ruling the same day (Trump v. Cook, No. 25A312), the Court denied the government's application to stay the preliminary injunction protecting Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, confirming Federal Reserve governors retain a different, more protective legal status. The opinion was revised and reposted July 1, 2026.
Primary source: Supreme Court of the United States — October Term 2025 Slip Opinions (official slip opinion list; opinion PDF at https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-322_new_4gcj.pdf) — https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/slipopinion/25
Relevant to: crypto exchanges, DCMs, prediction-market operators, stablecoin issuers, broker-dealers, and all entities regulated by the SEC or CFTC; CLARITY Act negotiations

entry.title: CLARITY Act placed on Senate Legislative Calendar No. 423; House Agriculture chair commits to fast follow; August recess is the operative deadline; seven Democratic votes remain the gap to cloture

category.term: U.S. Senate (Senate Banking Committee markup; Senate Legislative Calendar No. 423) / House Agriculture digital-assets subcommittee (Rep. Dusty Johnson statement)

entry.content:
The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act has been placed on the U.S. Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 423, eligible for a floor vote at any time Senate leadership chooses to schedule one, following a 15-9 Senate Banking Committee markup on May 14, 2026. As reported by The Defiant on June 19, 2026, House Agriculture digital-assets subcommittee chair Rep. Dusty Johnson stated on June 18 that the House will move immediately on a companion measure if the Senate passes the bill before the August recess, removing the need for a conference committee. The bill requires approximately 60 votes to clear a Senate filibuster — about seven Democratic votes beyond full Republican unity. Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.) has cited July 4 as a target; Sen. Cynthia Lummis has said August recess is more realistic; Galaxy Research has cut its passage-before-recess probability to 60%. Outstanding obstacles include an ethics-language dispute, stablecoin-yield rules, and a parallel lobbying campaign by gaming, tribal gaming, and labor groups demanding the bill include explicit language barring prediction markets from offering sports event contracts. The bill would assign digital commodities to CFTC spot-market authority, investment-contract assets to the SEC, and stablecoins to banking regulators under the GENIUS Act framework. Failure to pass before the August recess pushes the bill into a fall midterm calendar.
Coverage (reporting filing): The Defiant (June 19, 2026; reporting CLARITY Act Senate Calendar No. 423 placement, Rep. Johnson House fast-follow statement, and 7-Democrat cloture math) — https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/clarity-act-senate-floor-seven-democrat-math-house-fast-follow

entry.title: AGA, tribal gaming groups, and labor unions send Senate letter demanding CLARITY Act include explicit ban on prediction-market sports event contracts

category.term: American Gaming Association, Indian Gaming Association, AFL-CIO Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, UNITE HERE (coalition letter to U.S. Senate, June 16, 2026)

entry.content:
On June 16, 2026, a coalition led by the American Gaming Association (AGA), the Indian Gaming Association, the AFL-CIO's Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, and UNITE HERE sent a letter to the U.S. Senate urging legislators to amend the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act to include explicit language barring prediction markets from offering sports and casino-style event contracts. As reported by The Defiant, the letter states that prediction markets have 'fueled the largest expansion of gambling in U.S. history over the past 18 months, without voter approval or legislative authorization,' and the AGA has separately estimated states have lost roughly $1 billion in gaming tax revenue to prediction markets since the start of 2025.

entry.title: Kentucky AG sues Kalshi, Polymarket, and VGW alleging illegal unlicensed gambling operations

category.term: Kentucky Office of the Attorney General (Russell Coleman) — Franklin Circuit Court

entry.content:
On June 17, 2026, Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman filed lawsuits in Franklin Circuit Court against prediction-market operators Kalshi and Polymarket and against online sweepstakes-casino operator VGW (operator of Chumba Casino, Global Poker, and LuckyLand Slots), alleging the companies are conducting illegal, unlicensed gambling operations within the Commonwealth. As reported by Covers (and corroborated by Gambling Insider, Gambling News, LEX18, Yogonet, PlayUSA, and LINK nky), the suits allege Kalshi and Polymarket are effectively operating sportsbooks in Kentucky without the licenses required of regulated sports-betting operators and provide inadequate responsible-gambling protections. The suits seek temporary and permanent injunctive relief and all recoverable damages available to the Commonwealth.

entry.title: CFTC amends its Illinois lawsuit and seeks a preliminary injunction against the state's new 'exchange wager' prediction-market tax

category.term: CFTC — U.S. District Court, Northern District of Illinois

entry.content:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission amended its lawsuit against the State of Illinois (N.D. Illinois, No. 1:26-cv-03659, originally filed April 2, 2026) after Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker signed a budget creating a new tax structure for prediction markets. The amended complaint challenges Illinois's new 'exchange wager' provisions, arguing the state is attempting to regulate event-contract markets that fall within the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act; the new Illinois law would impose transaction fees ranging from 1.75% to 3.5% on sports event contracts. The CFTC also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction seeking to block Illinois from enforcing its gambling laws against event contracts while the litigation proceeds.

entry.title: Proposed class action alleges Robinhood runs an unlicensed sports-gambling operation through its prediction-markets hub

category.term: Matthew Mazza (plaintiff) — U.S. District Court, Northern District of California

entry.content:
On June 10, 2026, a proposed class action (Mazza v. Robinhood) was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against Robinhood Markets, Inc. and its subsidiary Robinhood Derivatives, alleging the company operates an unlicensed, illegal sports-gambling operation marketed as an investment product through its 'prediction markets hub.' The complaint alleges Robinhood's sports event contracts are effectively sports wagers, that the platform let customers bet against margin using existing stock holdings without clearly disclosing the risk at the point of trade, and that Robinhood created a misleading impression the products had state regulatory approval. The named plaintiff alleges he lost approximately $400,000 in fees, commissions, and wagers in 2025-2026.

entry.title: Cayuga Nation sues Caesars Sportsbook over mobile bets placed on tribal land — first tribal lawsuit against licensed sportsbook; novel IGRA 'where is the bet placed' geolocation theory

category.term: Cayuga Nation (plaintiff) — U.S. District Court, Northern District of New York

entry.content:
On June 16, 2026, the Cayuga Nation of New York filed a federal lawsuit in the Northern District of New York against American Wagering, Inc. (d/b/a Caesars Sportsbook), alleging that Caesars accepted mobile sports wagers from people physically located on the Cayuga reservation between January 8, 2022 and July 15, 2025, without tribal authorization, a gaming compact, or federal oversight. The complaint alleges violations of the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA): it argues that a mobile sports wager is placed at the bettor's physical location, not at the operator's server, and therefore betting accepted from within the reservation constitutes Class III gaming on Indian lands, requiring a tribal gaming ordinance and a federally approved tribal-state compact that the Cayuga Nation does not have for sports betting.

entry.title: U.S. Senate passes 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644) with statutory Fed CBDC ban through 2030; House concurrence vote pending

category.term: U.S. Senate

entry.content:
On June 18, 2026, the U.S. Senate invoked cloture (84-8) and passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644). The bill includes a provision banning the Federal Reserve from issuing or creating a central bank digital currency (CBDC) or any substantially similar asset, directly or through an intermediary, through December 31, 2030. The CBDC ban defines a CBDC as a dollar-denominated digital asset that is U.S. currency, a direct liability of the Federal Reserve System, and widely available to the public; it carves out dollar-denominated, open, permissionless, and private digital currencies with privacy protections comparable to physical U.S. currency.

entry.title: W.D. Michigan denies Robinhood preliminary injunction — sports event contracts are NOT swaps; CEA does not clearly preempt state gambling law

category.term: U.S. District Court, W.D. Michigan (Judge Paul Maloney)

entry.content:
On June 18, 2026, U.S. District Judge Paul Maloney of the Western District of Michigan denied Robinhood's motion for a preliminary injunction against Michigan state gambling enforcement in a second, near-identical ruling to the Polymarket denial issued the same day. The court held on two independent grounds: (1) sports event contracts of the type Robinhood offers are not 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act, placing them outside the CFTC's exclusive swap jurisdiction; and (2) even if the contracts were swaps, it is not clearly established that the CEA would preempt Michigan's state gambling law in this context. Together with the same-day Polymarket ruling, these are the first federal court holdings that sports event contracts fall outside the CEA swap definition.

entry.title: CME Group sues CFTC over approval of perpetual bitcoin futures (BTCPERP) on Kalshi — argues perps are swaps not futures; challenges 24-hour self-certification as APA violation

category.term: CME Group — U.S. District Court

entry.content:
CME Group filed suit against the CFTC challenging the agency's June 2026 approval of 24/7 perpetual bitcoin futures contracts (BTCPERP) on KalshiEx via the CFTC's Regulation 40.2 self-certification process. CME's complaint argues: (1) perpetual futures contracts are 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act rather than futures, and the CFTC therefore lacked authority to approve them as futures on a designated contract market; and (2) using the 24-hour self-certification process for a novel product violated the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements.

entry.title: CFTC enters final consent order against Celsius Network and CEO Mashinsky — civil fraud, CEL token manipulation, and unregistered pool charges resolved; DOJ criminal case continues
entry.content:
On June 18, 2026, the CFTC entered a final consent order against Celsius Network LLC and its former CEO Alex Mashinsky resolving civil enforcement claims arising from the 2022 collapse of the Celsius crypto-lending platform. The consent order resolves three enforcement theories: (1) fraudulent misrepresentation of deposit safety and liquidity practices to retail customers; (2) market manipulation through coordinated trading in Celsius's native CEL token, which the CFTC classified as a commodity; and (3) operating as an unregistered commodity pool operator (CPO) without CFTC registration. The DOJ's separate criminal case against Mashinsky continues.

entry.title: Five federal agencies propose a customer identification program rule for payment stablecoin issuers (GENIUS Act)

category.term: Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC, NCUA, and Treasury (FinCEN)

entry.content:
On June 18, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board — jointly with the OCC, FDIC, NCUA, and Treasury/FinCEN — requested comment on a proposed rule that would require certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) to maintain an effective customer identification program (CIP), with requirements comparable to those for banks and credit unions, implementing the GENIUS Act. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr issued a statement saying the GENIUS Act framework 'does not do enough so far to address the risks of illicit finance conducted through secondary market transactions in payment stablecoins.'

entry.title: Illinois enacts first-in-nation digital-asset transaction tax (SB 3019 / Digital Asset Tax Act)

category.term: State of Illinois (Gov. JB Pritzker)

entry.content:
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed Senate Bill 3019, the Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA), as part of the state's $55.9 billion budget, making Illinois the first U.S. state to impose a transaction-based tax on digital-asset activity. The law imposes a 0.2% privilege tax on brokers who exchange, transfer, or store digital assets for customers in the state; it applies to brokers with a physical presence in Illinois or an economic nexus (more than $100,000 in gross receipts from Illinois customers), takes effect January 1, 2027, and is projected to generate roughly $60 million.

entry.title: Congress folds a statutory Fed CBDC ban (through 2030) into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644)

category.term: U.S. Senate Banking Committee (Congress)

entry.content:
On June 16, 2026, the leaders of the Senate Banking and House Financial Services Committees released updated bill text for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644). The package folds in a statutory ban on a Federal Reserve CBDC: it amends the Federal Reserve Act to provide that the Fed 'may not issue or create' a CBDC through December 31, 2030 and carves out dollar-denominated, open, permissionless, and private digital currencies with privacy protections comparable to physical U.S. currency. A prior version passed the Senate 89-10 in March and the House passed its amended version 396-13 in May.

entry.title: Tribal coalition files amicus briefs opposing CFTC/Kalshi preemption of tribal gaming laws

category.term: Tribal Amici (coalition of federally recognized tribes)

entry.content:

entry.title: W.D. Michigan denies Polymarket PI — court rules sports event contracts are NOT 'swaps' under the CEA; CEA may not preempt state gambling law even if they were

category.term: U.S. District Court, W.D. Michigan

entry.content:
On June 17, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan denied Polymarket's motion for a preliminary injunction against enforcement of Michigan state gambling law. The court held on two independent grounds: (1) sports event contracts of the type Polymarket offers are not 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act; and (2) even if the contracts were classified as swaps, it is not clearly established that the CEA would preempt Michigan's state gambling law. The ruling is the first federal court holding that sports event contracts fall outside the CEA swap definition — directly contrary to the CFTC's preemption position.
Coverage (reporting filing): SBC Americas (reporting the W.D. Michigan PI denial) — https://sbcamericas.com/2026/06/18/polymarket-denied-injunction-michigan/

entry.title: NYDFS proposes stablecoin regulation aligning New York's framework with the federal GENIUS Act
entry.content:
On June 9, 2026, the New York State Department of Financial Services, under Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow, proposed a regulation to build on New York's existing stablecoin framework and align it with the federal GENIUS Act. The proposal carries forward DFS's prior requirements for U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins and adds new federal provisions, including setting maximum reserve amounts at any one custodian and requiring issuers to adopt risk-management programs. The final regulation would take effect at the same time as the GENIUS Act becomes effective, with a one-year transition period for existing New York-licensed issuers.
Primary source: NYDFS Press Release (June 9, 2026) — https://www.dfs.ny.gov/reports_and_publications/press_releases/pr20260609
Relevant to: stablecoin issuers, virtual-currency (BitLicense) licensees, custodians, payment-stablecoin platforms

entry.content:

entry.title: Pennsylvania Supreme Court rules skill games are slot machines; 120-day enforcement stay issued

category.term: Pennsylvania Supreme Court

entry.content:
On June 15, 2026, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court issued its majority opinion in J-97-2025 (Pace-O-Matic v. Pennsylvania), ruling that skill game machines 'are subject to both the Gaming Act and the Crimes Code,' overturning a Commonwealth Court ruling the Justices called 'deeply flawed.' The Court issued a 120-day enforcement stay during which law enforcement cannot take action against owners and operators. An estimated 70,000+ skill game machines operate in bars, VFWs, restaurants, and fraternal clubs statewide.

entry.content:
